findings.reason: Faulty parallelism in a series. Once the preposition is repeated (in … in …), it has to be repeated before every item; otherwise use it only once. As printed, the third item drops 'in', so 'popular tales and the ritual dramas of films' reads as a single object of the second 'in', and the three settings no longer match. Adding the third 'in' is the minimal fix, and students reciting the passage will learn the correct pattern.

Standard parallelism guidance (Garner, Chicago) says to use the preposition once or before every item, and a copy editor would mark the dropped one. As printed, 'popular tales and the ritual dramas of films' can read as one object of the second 'in'. That pairing makes no sense: the passage contrasts folk songs and popular tales, as folk forms, with film. Adding 'in' is the smallest fix and is clearly correct. I could not find the original source online to compare.

findings.reason: New reason to reopen this earlier decision. The decision says Fitzgerald's own text reads 'the gypsies', but that looks wrong. Every published edition I could find reads 'Suddenly one of these gypsies, in trembling opal, seizes a cocktail out of the air…' (The Great Gatsby, ch. 3). An exact-phrase web search for 'one of these gypsies, in trembling opal' returns Gatsby ch. 3 texts (LitCharts, Standard Ebooks, Toronto Pressbooks, americanliterature.com). The same search with 'the gypsies' finds nothing from Gatsby. The exam image (2016_p4) prints 'one of the gypsies', so this is the exam's misquotation, not a transcription slip. It matters for meaning: 'these' points back to ¶6's 'wanderers, confident girls', who are the 'gypsies'. 'The gypsies' is a definite noun phrase with nothing to refer to, because no gypsies have been mentioned. A copy editor checking the quotation against its source would mark it.

va.why: The 'current' text matches the file exactly. The new reason is correct and definite, and it shows the earlier decision ('Fitzgerald's text is the gypsies') rested on a wrong premise. The transcriptions of the 1925 Scribner first edition all read 'Suddenly one of these gypsies, in trembling opal, seizes a cocktail out of the air': Project Gutenberg #64317, the UVA anthology edition (based on that transcription), Standard Ebooks, Gutenberg Canada and the La Laguna copy. 'The gypsies' turns up only in secondary quotations and school handouts, so it is the exam's misquotation, not deliberate style. On grammar alone, 'the gypsies' could just pass as an epithet pointing back to ¶6's wanderers. But here the author's published text is the standard, and students will memorise this passage as Fitzgerald's words. Unlike the deliberate 'shorn' adaptation, changing 'these' to 'the' serves no purpose and weakens the explicit link to ¶6's 'wanderers, confident girls'. 'These' also matters for sense: it is what links the metaphor back to ¶6's 'wanderers, confident girls'. With 'the', the phrase has no antecedent. Restore 'these'.
